question: What share of older people with dementia in high-income health systems carry a dementia diagnosis? P-1046 measures it for US Medicare beneficiaries aged 65+ in 2015-2019 from claims, against an HRS-model expected prevalence. P-977 (World Alzheimer Report 2016) states it for 'most HIC' generally. The printed HIC figure has no source attached: the three references on that sentence are LMIC studies. The shared question holds only at the level of 'HIC older adults'. P-977's figure is not specific to the US or the period, and it is an assertion in a policy report, not a study result.
metric: Doubtful. P-1046's 'detection rate' is observed claims prevalence over model-expected prevalence (O/E). It counts every coded diagnosis, can exceed 1, and above 1 its authors read it as overdiagnosis. P-977's 'diagnostic coverage' is the proportion of people living with dementia who have received a diagnosis, bounded at 1. P-1046's authors treat the two as one metric: they set their 1.09 against a 38% US meta-analysis and a 62% NHS England figure. By construction, though, they differ in the numerator: all coded diagnoses against diagnosed true cases.

figures.P-1046: Dementia O/E 1.086, 1.093, 1.104 over the three 3-year windows 2015-2019 (printed), on 38.7 to 41.2 million beneficiaries per window. No interval is printed, and the sampling uncertainty is negligible at that size. The dominant uncertainty is the expected-rate model. Using the other US prevalence estimates the paper itself cites as denominators, with observed 0.096: 0.096/0.113 = 0.85 (Rajan) and 0.096/0.100 = 0.96 (Manly), against 1.10 with its own expected 0.086. Its lowest subgroups are Black 0.696, Hispanic 0.758 and dual-eligible 0.855.
figures.P-977: 'In most HIC, only 40-50% of people living with dementia have received a diagnosis', with no source, sample or interval printed for the HIC figure, so no interval can be derived. Its sourced figures, from a systematic review of 15 primary-care studies mainly in Europe and North America: PCP identification 73.4% (95% CI 62.6-82.9%); diagnosis recorded in notes 37.9% (26.8-49.6%).
figures.difference_and_reconciliation_arithmetic: Every P-1046 value (1.09 headline, 0.85-0.96 on alternative denominators, 0.70-0.86 in the lowest subgroups) lies above 0.50 and outside both of P-977's printed intervals. The two figures could both hold only if most coded diagnoses fall on people outside the expected case pool: at coverage 0.45 with O/E 1.09, false positives would make up (1.09 - 0.45)/1.09 = 59% of claims diagnoses (54% at coverage 0.50). Neither paper measures that share. The linked-data estimate P-1046 cites (Zhu et al., 2.4% overdiagnosis) is from a third study, not from either paper.

matched_figure_check: No matched figure reconciles the pair. P-1046 reports no US coverage figure against an epidemiological prevalence with case-level linkage, and its alternative denominators (0.85-0.96) stay far above 40-50%. P-977 reports nothing for the US or for 2015-2019. Its only sourced, interval-bearing figures (73.4% recognition, 37.9% recorded) come from primary-care attenders given a research diagnosis, a different ascertainment, and both still exclude P-1046's values.

candidate_explanations.difference: Metric construction: O/E counts all coded diagnoses, including those the authors call overdiagnosis, against a model-expected prevalence; coverage counts diagnosed true cases.
candidate_explanations.quote: The O/E ratio can be interpreted as the proportion of expected cases that were diagnosed or the detection rate.

candidate_explanations.difference: Expected-rate denominator: a demographics-only HRS model whose expected dementia prevalence (0.086) is below other US estimates.
candidate_explanations.quote: it is possible that our model underpredicts dementia prevalence, because our expected rate of 0.086 is slightly lower than the rates reported for the US population aged 65 and older by Rajan et al. [38] (0.113) and Manly et al. [39] (0.100), which are closer to the observed rate of 0.096.

candidate_explanations.difference: Case ascertainment in claims: the algorithm may count people without dementia; under the original CCW algorithm the ratio would be 1.23.
candidate_explanations.quote: Based on the original CCW algorithm, the observed rate would have been 0.106 and the detection rate 1.23, suggesting a 23% rate of overdiagnosis.

candidate_explanations.difference: Population and era: US Medicare 2015-2019 against a generic 'most HIC' figure in a 2016 report, whose attached references are LMIC studies.
candidate_explanations.quote: Diagnostic coverage is low. In most HIC, only 40-50% of people living with dementia have received a diagnosis. In LMIC there are few available estimates, but diagnostic coverage is unlikely to exceed 5-10% in most settings3–5.

candidate_explanations.difference: Setting of P-977's sourced evidence: primary-care attenders given a research assessment, compared with the PCP's judgement or notes.
candidate_explanations.quote: The typical design of such studies is that older patients seen in primary care are given a research diagnostic assessment, and this is then compared with the PCPs contemporaneous clinical judgment, and/or recording of information suggesting a clinical diagnosis in primary care medical records.

reason: The numbers are far apart and nothing either paper prints reconciles them. P-1046's dementia detection is about 1.09 (0.85-0.96 on the other US prevalence denominators it cites), against P-977's 40-50% for 'most HIC' and its sourced 37.9%/73.4% primary-care figures. P-1046 itself calls its rate 'much higher' than earlier estimates. It stays borderline on two conditions. Condition 2: an O/E ratio that counts all coded diagnoses and exceeds 1 is not the same construct as a coverage proportion bounded at 1, and the two can coexist if most claims diagnoses fall outside the expected case pool, a share neither paper measures. Condition 1: P-977's headline figure is an unsourced, generic HIC assertion rather than a US study result for the same period.

quotes.quote: Dementia was diagnosed more frequently than expected (1.086 to 1.104) from 2015 to 2019, mostly in non-Hispanic White beneficiaries (1.367) compared with 0.696 in Black beneficiaries and 0.758 in Hispanic beneficiaries.
The O/E ratio can be interpreted as the proportion of expected cases that were diagnosed or the detection rate.

In contrast, dementia appears to be overdiagnosed in Medicare beneficiaries by about 10%, even when we used a more stringent identification algorithm modified following the publication by Festa et al. [19].

This dementia detection rate is much higher than the 38% reported by a meta-analysis of US-based studies prior to 2007 [29] and the July 2022 estimate of 62% from the National Health Service in England [30], but close to a 2.4% overdiagnosis rate estimated by Zhu et al., [11] which used 2012 HRS data linked to Medicare claims.

our expected rate of 0.086 is slightly lower than the rates reported for the US population aged 65 and older by Rajan et al. [38] (0.113) and Manly et al. [39] (0.100), which are closer to the observed rate of 0.096.

Diagnostic coverage is low. In most HIC, only 40-50% of people living with dementia have received a diagnosis. In LMIC there are few available estimates, but diagnostic coverage is unlikely to exceed 5-10% in most settings3–5.
In a systematic review of 15 such studies conducted mainly in Europe and North America, the pooled proportion of dementia cases identified by PCPs was 73.4% (95% CI: 62.6-82.9%)34.
Diagnoses were even less likely to have been recorded in the patient notes (37.9%, 95% CI: 26.8-49.6%).
